before: A Rust macro that displays a value and adds a new line.
after: Show text or values, then start a new line.

before: Rust spelling that creates a binding whose value may later be replaced.
after: Give a value a name and allow later changes through that name.

before: Rust code that computes a number, such as score * 3.
after: A piece of code that works out a number.

before: A Rust choice that runs a block according to a true-or-false condition.
after: Choose a path by checking whether a condition is true.

before: A Rust loop that checks its condition before every repetition.
after: Repeat a block while its test is true. Check before each turn.

before: The last expression without a semicolon can provide a Rust function’s result.
after: The last expression can give a function its answer when it has no final semicolon.

before: A selected set of compatible Rust language rules, independent of the compiler release number.
after: A set of Rust language rules chosen for a project. This is separate from the compiler's version.

before: A type defining how numbers are represented and which values and operations are supported.
after: A kind of number with rules for what it can hold and which calculations it supports.

before: A Unicode code point excluding surrogate code points; the kind of value represented by Rust char.
after: One Unicode code point except the reserved surrogate values. A Rust char holds one such value; a visible character can be made from several.

before: Binding tuple elements to names according to their positions.
after: Give names to the parts of a tuple by their positions.

before: A loop that can yield a result through break with a value.
after: A loop that can stop and give back a value with break.

before: The final expression of a Rust block whose value becomes the block’s result.
after: The last expression in a block. Without a final semicolon, its value becomes the block's answer.

before: Responsibility for a value and its eventual release, enforced through Rust’s rules.
after: An owner is responsible for a value. Rust uses ownership rules to decide when the value can be used or dropped.

before: Transferring ownership so the previous binding cannot keep using the moved value.
after: Pass ownership to a new place. The old place cannot keep using the moved value.

before: An explicit type-defined operation for creating another value, not necessarily a deep copy for every type.
after: Make another value using the type's clone operation. Cloning a String copies its text; some other types share what is inside.

before: A reference allowing shared read access while another binding remains the owner.
after: Let another part of the program read a value while its owner keeps it.

before: An exclusive reference permitting mutation while its access remains active.
after: Give one active reference permission to change a value.

before: The region during which a reference must remain valid and its borrowing restrictions apply.
after: The part of the program during which a borrow must stay valid.

before: An owned growable sequence whose initialized element count is distinct from its capacity.
after: An ordered collection that can grow or shrink.

before: A contiguous sequence of elements, often accessed through a borrowed reference such as &[T].
after: A view of neighboring items in a collection. A borrowed slice can show them without copying them.

before: An enum representing either a present Some value or explicit None absence.
after: A type with two cases: Some holds a value; None means no value is there.

before: Unwrapping success or returning a compatible failure to the caller.
after: A question mark after a Result takes out a success or sends the error back to the caller.

before: Ownership rules apply independently to owned fields inside a struct.
after: A struct's fields can have their own owners. Moving one field need not move the whole struct.

before: A method receiver borrowing exclusive mutable access to its object.
after: A method's way of borrowing its object so it can change that object.

before: Data carried by a particular enum variant.
after: Data carried by one case of an enum.

before: An additional Boolean condition on a match arm.
after: An extra true-or-false test that a match branch must pass.

before: A named behavior contract implemented by types.
after: A named set of behavior that a type can provide.

before: A compiler-generated trait implementation supported by a type’s fields.
after: Behavior that Rust writes automatically when the type's fields support it.

before: A type declaration parameterized by one or more type arguments.
after: A type with a placeholder for a type chosen when the code is used.

before: A dynamically dispatched value viewed through a compatible trait, here by borrowing.
after: A way to use a value through the behavior of a trait. The program can choose the matching method as it runs.

before: A contract relating how long borrowed inputs and outputs may be used.
after: A rule connecting how long an input view and a returned view may be used.

before: Rejecting references whose owners cannot remain alive for the required use.
after: Rust checks that a returned reference will not point to a value that has already gone away.

before: A stateful producer whose adapters do work as items are requested.
after: An iterator that waits for an item to be requested before doing its work.

before: Access to a variable from the environment of an anonymous function.
after: A closure's access to a name from the place where the closure was made.

before: A closure capturing its environment by value, with moves for non-Copy captures.
after: A closure that takes its captured values by value. A String moves into it instead of being borrowed.

before: The result type that determines how iterator items are gathered.
after: The result type tells collect how to gather the items.

before: A byte position between complete Unicode scalar encodings rather than inside one.
after: A position before or after a whole UTF-8 character value, not inside its bytes.

before: Access to an existing map value or an insertion point for a missing key.
after: A way to reach a map's existing value or supply one for a missing key.

before: A hash-based collection of unique values without stable iteration order.
after: A collection that keeps each distinct item once. Its order is not guaranteed.

before: Rules controlling which module paths can access an item.
after: Rules that say which code can use an item inside a module.

before: A Cargo dependency resolved from a supplied local directory.
after: A library that Cargo finds in a named folder rather than downloading it.

before: A test compiled as an external consumer of a library’s public interface.
after: A test that uses a library from the outside through its public code.

before: A typed failure representing a violated application rule, with intentionally chosen context.
after: An error that describes a problem with the task's own rules, such as minutes outside the allowed range.

before: Unique ownership of a heap allocation through an owning pointer with a finite-sized representation.
after: A Box is one owner of a value kept in separate storage.

before: Keeping an allocation alive while one or more strong owning pointers refer to it.
after: Several owners share one value. A count tracks how many owners are keeping it alive.

before: A value whose lifetime represents a currently active RefCell borrow.
after: A value that keeps a RefCell borrow active until that borrow is released.

before: Reference-counted ownership with thread-safe count updates, subject to the payload’s thread-safety bounds.
after: An Arc lets owners keep the same value alive across threads. It does not by itself allow them to change the value.

before: An owned lock token that provides protected access and releases the lock when dropped.
after: The value returned by locking a mutex. It controls access and unlocks when dropped.

before: A handle used to wait for a thread and observe its returned value or panic.
after: A handle for waiting for a worker thread and getting its result or failure.

before: The period during which sender handles can still produce messages; receiver iteration ends only after all senders are gone and queued values drained.
after: A receiving loop can finish after all senders are gone and all queued messages have been read.

before: Marker traits for safe transfer of ownership and safe sharing of references across threads, respectively.
after: Send allows a value to move between threads. Sync allows shared references to the value to cross threads.

before: Returning a failure to the caller rather than silently substituting a successful-looking value.
after: Send a failure back to the caller instead of continuing the failed task.

before: Reading and validating lines under explicit input-size, line-count and value limits.
after: Read lines while enforcing limits, such as how many lines are accepted and which numbers they may contain.

before: A platform-aware representation of a filesystem location, not proof that the location exists.
after: A value that describes a route to a file or folder. Creating a path does not create the file.

before: Checking the number and meaning of command-line values before relying on them.
after: Check that the inputs given at startup have the expected count and form.

before: The explicitly chosen normalization, syntax and domain rules determining which inputs are accepted.
after: The rule for deciding whether an input is allowed after it has been read.

before: User-facing formatting through a borrowed Formatter with a returned formatting Result.
after: The rule a type supplies for showing itself as readable text.

before: A value describing asynchronous work whose body does not progress until driven by polling.
after: Work that does not begin just because its future was created.

before: A deliberately limited poll of a known-ready future, not a runtime for arbitrary asynchronous work.
after: Ask a future once whether it has an answer. A ready future can answer on that poll.

before: The number of times an expanded macro causes a captured expression to execute.
after: How many times the code produced by a macro evaluates the supplied expression.

before: A safety obligation that must be upheld for an operation requiring unsafe, not a waiver of Rust’s validity rules.
after: Rules a caller must meet for an unsafe operation. A safe interface can check them before allowing the operation.

before: A finite sequence of parsing, domain filtering and capped collection with an explicit rejection policy.
after: A sequence of steps that checks data and limits how many results it keeps.
